title: code review refactoring and legacy modernization
concepts: Code review checks whether a change is correct, understandable, maintainable, and appropriate to its users. Reviewers should distinguish must-fix correctness or safety issues from preferences and future improvements.
Small, coherent changes are easier to reason about, test, review, and revert. A change description should state intent, important tradeoffs, and how it was verified.

Refactoring changes internal structure while preserving observable behavior. Use a characterization baseline and small safe transformations when tests are incomplete; refactoring is not a synonym for feature work or rewriting.
Legacy modernization balances delivery risk with long-term change cost. Map dependencies and critical behaviors, create seams and tests, and migrate incrementally where the business cannot pause.
Review is a collaborative exchange. Ask specific questions, explain impact, separate objective defects from style, and respond to feedback without treating disagreement as personal criticism.
Automated formatting, static analysis, tests, and security checks can enforce repeatable rules; human reviewers focus on design intent, edge cases, and maintainability.

scopeExclusions: Git branching and merge mechanics are covered in t09-002.
Detailed test suite architecture and coverage metrics are covered in t10-001 and t10-004.
Database schema migrations and data backfill implementation are covered by SQL Server and EF Core topics.
Language-specific compiler refactoring APIs and complete Fowler refactoring catalog are outside this bounded scope.
Organizational performance review and promotion processes are not code-review practices.
accuracyFacts: Refactoring is intended to preserve observable behavior; tests provide evidence but do not prove equivalence for unobserved behavior.
A change to a published interface may be behavior breaking even if internal callers were updated; unknown external consumers and serialized/runtime-discovered names expand the observable contract.
Incremental migrations may be irreversible after new writes or external side effects; a feature flag does not reverse persisted data.
Google code review terminology and workflow recommendations are organization-specific examples, not universal approval policy.
Shadow requests must not cause duplicate side effects; parallel-run and dual-write safety depends on explicit ownership and reconciliation.
